findings.summary: THE CLAUSE THAT REPLACED P21 RESTS ON A FALSE PREMISE ABOUT `CommitDelta`. The new text says the uncheckpointed tail 'is this row's BOUND to state and pin, not to close: a flushSeq committed after the ancestor's last checkpoint exists in no object, since `CommitDelta` carries no pod attribution', and the parent section repeats it as the reason M4.10d depends on M4.10b ('returning the original offsets across a takeover needs a carrier, and today there is none for a commit after the ancestor's last checkpoint'). Measured against the record: `CommitDelta(long sequence, List<SegmentCommit> segments)` and `SegmentCommit(String segmentKey, List<RunCommit> runs)` (format/src/main/java/binjava/format/CommitDelta.java:28,66), and `SegmentKey.render` emits `prefix/date/timestampMillis-podShortId-sequence-headerLen-filter` (format .../SegmentKey.java:163-169). Every delta therefore carries the producing pod's `podShortId` and a per-pod sequence inside the segment key, and each `RunCommit` carries `firstOffset`/`lastOffset` -- the original offsets themselves. The carrier the row says does not exist is the delta, and it sits exactly where the tail lives: M4.9 already reads newest-checkpoint-plus-at-most-K-deltas at recovery, so the bytes are on the successor's existing recovery path at zero extra requests. `Sequencer` (sequencer/.../Sequencer.java:78-81) already defines the answer as 'matched on ... its own segment', i.e. keyed on the segment key, not on flushSeq -- and this same M4.10d section relies on that when it demands 'ASSERT THAT NO DELTA CARRYING THE REPLAYED SEGMENT KEY WAS APPENDED'. The section thus asserts in one paragraph that the chain carries the replayed segment key and in another that no object carries the tail. Only the `flushSeq` FIELD is absent from the chain; that is a much narrower fact than the one the bound is built on.
findings.failure_scenario: A session picks up M4.10d, reads 'the uncheckpointed tail is this row's BOUND to state and pin, not to close', and writes an acceptance criterion asserting that a replay arriving after the ancestor's last checkpoint is NOT answered -- pinning a limitation the tree does not have. The retry after an ambiguous IOException, the one case M4.10 exists to make safe, is precisely the case that lands in that tail (the ambiguous PUT is the last thing the dying leader did), so the row documents the product's central scenario as out of scope while the deltas that would answer it are already being read. Worse, the pinned assertion becomes a tripwire: a later commit that closes the tail by matching the submitted segment key against the deltas M4.9 already replays now has to DELETE a landed assertion, which reads as the non-negotiable-2 / testing.md rule-5 inversion rather than as progress. REMEDY IS A DELETION, not more prose: strike the 'exists in no object, since CommitDelta carries no pod attribution' reason and the parent section's 'today there is none', and say only what is true -- the chain carries no `flushSeq`, so whether the tail is answerable turns on whether M4.10b keys on the segment key or on the pair.

findings.summary: THE NEW COST PROPERTY MISQUOTES THE RULE IT CITES, ON THE ONE AXIS THIS PROJECT EXISTS TO GET RIGHT. It reads 'No object-store REQUEST RATE may scale with pods, records, shards or partitions (non-negotiable 6)'. Non-negotiable 6 says: 'Request rates scale with segments, AZs and nodes -- never with records, shards, partitions or indices', and cost.md's invariant block states it as a two-column table with `nodes` on the PERMITTED side. An ingester is a K8s pod (AGENTS.md Vocabulary), so pods are nodes: cost.md R1 mandates 'Bundle all indices and partitions of a pod into one object per flush' and ADR-0017 is titled `every-pod-writes`, which makes the segment PUT rate pods/interval by design. So the property as written forbids the shipped architecture and attributes that prohibition to a non-negotiable that says the opposite about that axis; it also silently drops `indices`, the axis non-negotiable 6 does forbid and the one the whole product is named for. The bullet's own example is correct and is the rule that was meant -- 'a per-pod `ctl/pods/<podId>` object rewritten on every commit ... multiplies the COMMIT-PATH PUT rate by the pod count, which is what M4.7 removed' (verified: M4.7's archived row names the per-pod dimension as the one it built) -- i.e. the constraint belongs to the commit/metadata path, cost.md R6's family, not to all request rates. The GET half of the bullet is sound.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.10b is an ADR row, and this list is the constraint set its author is told the decision must satisfy. Read literally, the property rejects any design whose request count moves with pod count -- which includes the segment write path that already ships -- so the author either rejects a correct proposal or, more likely, concludes the property is unusable and weighs none of it, leaving the ADR with no request-rate analysis at all. The second outcome is the one this bullet was added in round 6 to prevent. It is also a false citation of the line AGENTS.md calls 'the architecture', copied into a row that will be read long after this round. Remedy: state it on the axis cost.md states it on -- the commit/metadata request rate is independent of pod count (R6, M4.7) and no request rate may scale with records, shards, partitions or indices (non-negotiable 6) -- and cite the R-number, which sdd.md rule 9 asks for and no rule here does.

findings.summary: ROUND 6 DELETED EVERY MECHANISM GUESS EXCEPT THE ONE IN THE PRESERVED TEXT, AND THAT ONE IS THE TRAP. The source row -- kept verbatim above the sub-sections, and re-published by this commit -- still says the fix belongs 'with whatever makes the pair durable (the lease's own epoch is the obvious candidate, and the sequencer already holds it)'. Nothing in M4.10b, c or d retracts or qualifies it, while the SegmentKey candidate one section below is explicitly fenced as 'A FACT TO WEIGH, NOT A CONCLUSION'. The asymmetry matters because the lease epoch is the SEQUENCER's leadership term, not the producing pod's incarnation. It discriminates a pod restart only while producer and sequencer are the same process -- true in M4, where `LocalSequencer` states 'a node that does not hold the lease gets an empty Optional here ... COMMIT FORWARDING IS M5's' -- and stops discriminating the moment M5's forwarding lands, which is the entire reason `CommitRequest` carries `podId` at all (M4.1's archived row: 'a forwarded commit (M5) is meaningless without the identity of the node that produced it'). M4.10d's own fixture already models the M5 shape: `CheckpointWriterContentTest` has `poda` and `podb` committing into ONE `CommitLog` at one epoch. So a key qualified by the lease epoch passes every test M4 can write, including all of M4.10d's, and then suppresses real commits at M5 -- and M4.10d itself names the discriminator this candidate fails ('THE DISCRIMINATOR IS A POD RESTART, NOT A TAKEOVER'), without ever connecting it to the candidate the same section preserves.
findings.failure_scenario: The M4.10b author opens `#m410b`, scrolls past the preserved row three paragraphs above it, and takes the only candidate the section calls 'obvious'. `(podId, flushSeq, leaseEpoch)` then passes M4.10d's whole suite because every M4 fixture has one committing process per epoch. At M5, pod A restarts under a leader whose epoch never moved, reissues flushSeq 0 for a NEW segment, and the dedup suppresses it -- the exact failure the row's own headline calls 'worse than the duplication it exists to prevent', shipped with green tests and an accepted ADR behind it. Remedy is one clause, and a deletion is enough: either strike the parenthetical from the preserved row or add to M4.10b that the lease epoch is the sequencer's term and does not move when a producing pod restarts, so it discriminates only for as long as producer and sequencer are one process.

findings.summary: 'Four properties the decision must satisfy' is followed by FIVE bullets -- the count was not updated when the request-rate property was added this round, and the very next clause says 'five rounds ... five falsifiable guesses', so the mismatch reads as deliberate. Compounding it, M4.10b's own backlog row names only three of the five ('ANSWERED with its original offsets ... must not make any object grow with history (ADR-0033); must survive a checkpoint truncating the walk and a leader change'); the format property is implied by the row's headline, but the request-rate property -- the only one naming a non-negotiable -- appears nowhere in the row. This is the countable-claim failure the tree's own `rounds:M0.76` entry records four times over, in the commit whose entire content is prose.
findings.failure_scenario: A reader of the constraint list cannot tell whether the fifth bullet is a property the ADR must satisfy or commentary appended after the list was closed, and the summary row -- the thing read first, and the only thing read if the notes link is not followed -- does not restate it. The cost property is then the one plausibly dropped, which is the property added to close round 6's finding. One word fixes the heading; the row is a summary and can stay as it is, but if a property is worth naming in the row at all, non-negotiable 6 is the one.

findings.summary: 'the durable half today is `Checkpoint.pods`, one uvarint per pod' overstates what the paragraph is weighing, and 'half' has no antecedent -- the sentence sits inside a list of `SegmentKey.render`'s three components, so 'half' reads as one of those and is not. `Checkpoint.pods` is durable in the sense that the bytes are on the store, but it is never read back: `CheckpointWriter` starts every leader with an empty map (its own javadoc: 'its first checkpoint carries no pods at all -- emptying the idempotency window'), which is exactly the gap `CheckpointWriterContentTest.theFirstCheckpointAfterATakeoverCarriesNoPodsAtAll` pins and exactly what M4.10d's fold exists to close. Also, `SegmentPublisher`'s 'unique WITHOUT coordination' is said of the whole KEY (pod id plus per-pod sequence), not of the sequence alone, as the attribution here reads.
findings.failure_scenario: The M4.10b author reads 'the durable half today is Checkpoint.pods' as meaning the flushSeq side already survives, weighs only the SegmentKey side as open, and produces an ADR that assumes a recovered window it has not asked anyone to build -- while M4.10d, which owns the fold, is a separate commit that may land after it. Naming it 'written but never recovered' says the same thing without the assumption.
